walkthroughs.body_html:
Animal Physiology — a core area of Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Animal Physiology brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Animal Physiology.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Burnet's clonal selection theory of immunity dates from:

options: Inserting aquaporins in collecting duct
Closing aquaporins
Increasing glomerular filtration
Stimulating renin

mcqs.q: How does myelination increase the speed of nerve impulse conduction?
options: Action potentials jump between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), skipping the myelinated sections.
Myelin makes the axon thicker so the signal travels faster through more material.
Negative feedback stops the body from responding to any internal change.
Myelin contains additional ion channels that speed up depolarisation.

mcqs.q: Where do plants get most of their biomass from?
options: Negative feedback stops the body from responding to any internal change.
Plants get most of their mass from the soil through their roots.
From carbon dioxide in the air — the carbon in plant tissue comes mostly from CO2 fixed during photosynthesis.
Plants gain most of their mass directly from sunlight, which has weight.

mcqs.q: What does negative feedback do in homeostasis?
options: Negative feedback makes a process get worse or amplifies the change.
It reverses a change in a controlled variable, bringing it back towards the set point.
Myelin contains additional ion channels that speed up depolarisation.
Negative feedback stops the body from responding to any internal change.
